*Query*

{noformat}    with model_params as 
    (
    Select *, DATE(LEAD(from_date, 1, date('9999-12-31')) OVER (PARTITION BY city, platform, channel ORDER BY DATE(from_date))) AS end_date
    FROM 
      (
      Select city, platform, channel, DATE(modelling_date) AS from_date,
      vmax_mean, lam_mean, case when has_experiment=1 then 'model+exp' else 'model' end as measurement_state
      from ng_fivetran_google_sheets_marketing.rider_mmm_curve_parameters
      UNION ALL 
      Select city, platform, channel, DATE(modelling_date) AS from_date,
      vmax_mean, lam_mean, measurement_state
      from ng_fivetran_google_sheets_marketing.rider_attribution_curve_parameters
      )
    )
    Select *

Hey [~accountid:641d5e830e6828ab20269e6d] ,
Thank you for your response. 
I want to clarify a bit the lifecycle of a basket:

# An *active basket* is *created* when a user adds an item from the app. Each basket is specific to a provider (restaurant, bolt market, etc). If the user visits another provider and adds an item, we will create another basket tied to that specific provider. The old basket becomes *expired (abandoned) basket*.
An active basket can also be created from a *closed basket*. Check step 3 for how a basket can become closed.
# If a basket is not updated for 2 days we will mark the basket as *expired (abandoned) basket*.
# If the user wants to create an order using an *active basket*, we will mark the basket as *closed basket* and we will create an order (with the associated order id) from it.

!image-20240605-075105.png|width=351,height=162,alt="image-20240605-075105.png"!

Now let’s think about each basket type and where we use it in app.

h3. Active basket

Active baskets are used to display various information about the basket on the checkout screen. Please note that an active basket is always no older than 2 days.

We do store various information such as delivery location, active campaigns and basket items.

*_I don’t think it’s feasible to delete active baskets as they are used in various places in the app and are transitioned to expired after 2 days._*

h3. Expired (abandoned) basket

Once a basket is expired, it will never be used again by the user. We still do need to keep those basket for 4 months because fraud team is using them, however, as [~accountid:62680739b31e6f0068621332] already mentioned we do have an initiative to delete older than 4 months baskets.

*_I will ask fraud if we can reduce this period. Is keeping expired (abandoned) baskets for 4 months an issue?_*

h3. Closed baskets

We need to keep closed baskets for multiple reasons:

# We need to show the order information on the order progress screen. Usually, all our orders are delivered in one day.
# We need to show all past orders and their contents (that means basket) to the user under the {{Orders}} screen.
# We also want to allow the user to quickly reorder the same items, so again we need to keep the information about the content that they ordered
# We also want to keep older baskets for allowing users to open CS disputes, as order might miss some items, have wrong items or have damaged items.

Some screenshots from the app that use the information stored in closed baskets:

!image-20240605-081947.png|width=531,height=1150,alt="image-20240605-081947.png"!



!image-20240605-082034.png|width=50%,alt="image-20240605-082034.png"!

*_Is deleting closed baskets that resulted in an order a requirement?_*

As a user, I would expect that the app should keep a list of orders already made.

Hello,  [~accountid:62bff85c118b20bee2bdca35] As confirmed by our local accounting partner, a section in the CIT return includes details of the top five earners and their remunerations, as required by the French tax authorities.

However, the Financial Statements submitted to the Trade Register do not include this sensitive information, and the CIT return itself is not filed there.

If a third-party request is received for the CIT return (e.g. bank or some other institution), the sheet containing the top 5 earners (sheet "2067") can and should be removed to comply with GDPR.

Therefore, salary information is not made public (only to the tax authorities),  the CIT return and Financial Statements are filed to different institutions. Hence, we recommend starting filing the Financial Statements for FY2023 with the local registry.

Please share your thoughts. Thank you and best wishes, Karoli

Hi Janeli!

Thanks for the detailed response, and providing even further context - this really helps to triage the issue to get to a better. Your technical skills are very good - we’re here for the nerdy stuff and you’re the experts in AP activities 😎 🤝 

Invoice without cost center in Workday should not have gone through to payment, I agree with you there Janneli. I’ve just checked, and there isn’t a rule to ensure that Cost Center, Business Line or Region are mandatory when submitting the supplier invoice - we’ll get that added, just doing a quick impact assessment. 

{quote}The issue is still most likely that the coding rules have incorrect CC or missing CC or AP simply forgets it. And yes, a lot of the approvers do not check the codings at all and are approving without it.{quote}

Ok, this does seem like an operational issue rather than technical. We would expect that every AP Specialist inserts the required dimensions, and approvers are checking it - but that’s not the case. We can add a validation on the Workday side here. 

{quote}I’m sorry I actually do not understand the difference. If the CC is not found in Workday (even if it is empty in Telema) why cannot it be sent back via a validation and with ERP complained status? To me (not maybe technically so bright) it seems the logic is for example similar to the posting date validation. In that case, WD can send it back with ERP complained status that the posting date cannot be used, so would really want the same for cost centers (and other mandatory data).{quote}

The way that the integration works is the following: 

# The integrations checks which invoices are eligible for being picked up i.e. “sent to flow” 
# The integration has mapping logic, which fields to map where. If a field in Telema is mapped against Workday field (through Reference IDs and mappings tables) then it will aim to insert that.
# If all data can be populated successfully in the supplier invoice in Workday (including missing fields) and Workday essentially accepts that format - it will then aim to create the invoice. At this point we can kick in validation before invoice goes into APPROVED state such as: “incorrect cost center, missing cost center, missing tax, missing attachment, wrong tax applicability” or if the posting period is not open, it cannot be created in a closed period. So think of it as the integration is not even able to *kick off* the process, and gets the error when a human would try to press *submit*  in Workday. This is where ERP complained status comes in. 

My proposal here is the following, in light of all the issues, and activities that we are doing : both with Telema as a tool, integration and SIWA / Approvals in Workday.

We will add the following validations in Workday:

* Cost Center is mandatory.
* Business Line is mandatory 
* Region is mandatory
* Spend Category is mandatory 

This means, that *if* an invoice came in, without ANY of these values, the value would have to be added on the Workday side, and then the invoice will be able to be submitted. I understand it is not exactly what has been requested here - i.e.. ERP complained status but it is a functional/operational item, not integration. 

My strongest recommendation that we enable Supplier Invoice Work Area into production, and that will allow you and your team to see *all* invoices in draft (if something was caused to be in draft). I would like to present this to you over a quick 30 minute call.

We can enable the supplier invoice work area, without having approvals yet live but they will come into it in the near-future. This would be in line with the things that we have been working on. What do you think?

Thank you for reaching out.

This issue has been discussed in several Slack channels. Unfortunately, it's quite challenging for us to manage this specific type of automation refund abuse while cash is not yet part of the balance flow. In Rides, cash transactions are not integrated with the balance system. As a result, when a ride is reported as unpaid, customers are not charged (the rider balance does not go to negative), and therefore, they don't have a reason to complain about potential driver dishonesty. In short, we can't determine the legitimacy of these reports. It ultimately depends on Customer Support processes to decide when and how much to compensate drivers. Each market has its own compensation guidelines. Regarding the orders refunded by AI you can reach out to CS-product team to turn off that for the market or changing something in the AI patterns but I am sure they are already aware of the situation. Our ability to address this from a Fraud perspective is limited.

Article 211 (Grounds for termination) of the Public Sector Contract Law says:

# _The following are grounds for termination of the contract:_

_a) The death or incapacity of the individual contractor or the extinction of the legal personality of the contracting company, without prejudice to what is provided for in Article 98 regarding contractor succession._ 

_b) The declaration of bankruptcy or insolvency in any other procedure._ 

_c) Mutual agreement between the Administration and the contractor._ 

_d) Delay in meeting deadlines by the contractor. In any case, unjustified delay in the execution of the work plan established in the specifications or in the contract, in any activity, for a period exceeding one-third of the initial term of the contract, including any possible extensions._

_e) Delay in payment by the Administration for a period exceeding that established in section 6 of Article 198 or the lower period established under section 8._ 

_f) Non-compliance with the main obligation of the contract. Also considered grounds for termination of the contract are the non-fulfillment of other essential obligations provided that these have been so qualified in the specifications or in the corresponding descriptive document, provided that the following two requirements are met:_

# _That they respect the limits established for freedom of agreement in section 1 of Article 34._
# _That they are precisely, clearly, and unequivocally listed in the specifications or in the descriptive document, with general clauses not being admissible._ 

_g) The impossibility of executing the provision under the initially agreed terms when it is not possible to modify the contract in accordance with Articles 204 and 205; or when, given the circumstances established in Article 205, the modifications involve, individually or collectively, alterations to the price of the contract, in an amount exceeding, up or down, 20 percent of the initial contract price, excluding Value Added Tax._ 

_h) Those specifically indicated for each category of contract in this Law.*_ 

_i) Non-payment, during the execution of the contract, of salaries by the contractor to the workers participating in it, or the non-compliance with the conditions established in the collective agreements in force for these workers also during the execution of the contract._

# _In cases where there are several grounds for termination of the contract with different effects regarding the economic consequences of termination, priority shall be given to the one that has appeared first in time._



Based on the article excerpted above, it appears that the bidder cannot unilaterally terminate the contract but must do so with the agreement of the Public Administration. I anticipate that if we breach the contract by terminating it unilaterally without a cause, we may be required to indemnify the city, or they may pursue damages against us. 

If you require a more detailed risk assessment, please inform me. However, I may not be able to provide it by the end of the week due to the heavy workload I’m currently experiencing.

*the contract we are discussing does not have a specific regulation in that law.

Happy to discuss further if this help.

Many thanks.

Additionally, I am including below the feedback provided by external counsel via email:

_As initially drafted, the agreement can lead, among others, to the following commercial and legal issues:_

 

* _Given that the last year of the agreement is the one where the repayment of the €1 million can take place, there is a risk that such payment does not occur if Mobility has a negative EBIT, except if such payment is regulated as a fix payment irrespective of Mobility's EBIT. We have adjusted the language in this sense, although we understand that the operations team may be open to assume such risk._

 

* _It may be convenient to delete, to the extent possible, any cross-reference to the agreements executed by third parties having an impact on this agreement. Particularly, if Mobility's intention is to have Bolt acting indirectly like a 'guarantor' before Tibus to ensure the payment of €1,200 per VTC per month. As already conveyed, if that's the idea pursued by Mobility, the structure to be followed should be a tri-party agreement (Tibus, Mobility, Bolt) , particularly to properly ensure Bolt's position/exposure and to properly regulate any triggers.-->_ {color:#ff5630}BL: My understanding is that a tri-party agreement is not feasible since Mobility prefers not to disclose the Bolt -Mobility commercial relationship{color} {color:#ff5630}to Tibus.{color}

 

* _We would recommend regulating the upfront payment as an escrow or establish a similar structure, not obliging Bolt to transfer the funds directly to Mobility. Any potential breach of the agreement by Mobility may lead to Bolt losing the relevant monies. It would be good that a Bolt team assesses Mobility's financial capability to ensure repayment._

Hi Sam, 



Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on May 6th, 2024.



After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your request, we have determined that we do not process personal data in relation to your location between April 21, 2024 to April 29, 2024. 

We take your privacy seriously. As a part of this commitment, we would like to clarify our practices of collecting your location information. 

We start collecting your location data when you grant your permission for tracking it ‘All time', ‘While using the App’ or ‘Once’ via the application that refers to the settings on your devices. We ask for permission on sign in; however, such permission can be revoked or granted at any time via your device settings either when a prompt to authorise background use is displayed in the Bolt app or on your own. Your location is collected only in the foreground. It means that we start collecting your location data when you open the Bolt app and stop collecting it when you close the Bolt app. 

The permission to share your location data ‘All the time’ applies only to the geofencing feature which is used to notify you if we are operating in the specific area. We do not, however, store any of your location data in relation to this. iOS and Android devices enable apps to automatically trigger notifications when the user enters a specific geographical area. This does not require for the Bolt app to run in the background or mobile data to be used. Apple and Android store this information at their end and automatically trigger those notifications when a user enters a defined area, without sharing the user’s location with Bolt.

Hi [~accountid:5fa01e19aea468006a8a298e], an NDA as such is designed for a negotiation between the parties prior to entering into a commercial agreement (e.g., supply agreement). So the confidential information disclosed relates to all business and operational discussions and disclosures therefore not tied to any-one particular purpose between the parties. Therefore, Bolt cannot completely warrant every discussion or disclosure made under the NDA is correct.

Once the parties pass the NDA phase and start negotiating a commercial agreement, then the information disclosed for the purpose of scoping the project is narrowed down and can be relied upon, and in case of mistakes the agreed scope can be adjusted. We’re just not at that phase yet with the NDA.

Answering your point about the dispute - the Supplier will not bear responsibility for wrong information supplied by Bolt, but neither will Bolt. Naturally Bolt will provide the most accurate information it can, but can’t simply guarantee 100% accuracy at this phase. The Supplier should know that such information may need to be reviewed before entering into a commercial agreement (e.g., supply agreement).

We can have scooters in Workday as assets, but here’s some things to consider: 

Loading them one by one should perhaps be considered to do via API rather than manual EIB because of the time consumption. I have not discussed this with Dominika. 

Maintenance: 

* How detailed and up to date should the information about scooters be? How often do we need to update locations on them? +This currently can be done via EIB.+ 
* Are they written off on a monthly-weekly-daily basis? +Currently this can be done via EIB+ and this is quite a lot of manual work and timeconsuming. 

Scooter batches: 

Can upload them as one big asset: 

!image-20240606-062123.png|width=1227,height=1120,alt="image-20240606-062123.png"!

Different life scenarios: 

* we dispose some of them - then accounting would need to manually edit the asset. [~accountid:6131df23b1894f00718e9faa] can comment here what the process would be if we want to dispose part of the giant asset.
* still, question of locations remains? 
* yes, quantity is marked as 250, but overall it still behaves as one asset. 



*What else can Workday do?*

*Composite Assets* 

You can register 2 types of composite assets:

* Discrete composite assets contain asset components that maintain their own costs, depreciation, and lifecycle events. Workday tracks separate lifecycle events for these assets.
* Nondiscrete composite assets contain asset components that maintain the same costs, depreciation, and lifecycle events. Workday tracks the same lifecycle event for these assets. Also, each asset that is part of a nondiscrete composite asset exists in reference only.

Example: You might want to use a camera, lens, and tripod together. You can register all 3 assets as 1 composite asset. Workday populates the acquisition method of composite assets with _Composed_

Conclusion: could be used for scooters if we have battery and scooter separately and want them together. 



*Pooled Assets* 

I set up Asset Pooling Rule: 



!image-20240606-063141.png|width=1354,height=243,alt="image-20240606-063141.png"!

Registered the asset: 

!image-20240606-063843.png|width=1306,height=1117,alt="image-20240606-063843.png"!

Still behaves like regular asset (and it should): 

!image-20240606-063857.png|width=907,height=598,alt="image-20240606-063857.png"!

Copy-paste from Workday guidelines: 

Pooled assets are groups of similar tangible items that you register and track as a single asset in Workday. Example: 100 flash drives. Pooling assets is useful for tracking multiple low-value assets and enables you to keep your asset register clean and maintainable. You can pool assets that you register manually or assets that Workday registers from lines on receipts or supplier invoices. You can't pool assets that you create by capitalizing project transactions.

Pooled assets follow the asset book rules, and are subject to the Spend account posting rule. You can place pooled assets in service, and depreciate a capitalized pooled asset as a single asset. Asset lifecycle events equally apply to each asset included in the pool.

Bolt fully assumes responsibility for its processing activities and adherence to applicable laws, including the GDPR. This covers areas such as engaging subprocessors, implementing necessary security measures, and establishing data retention periods._

_When a business customer`s employee or any data subject uses Bolt Business services for a ride, they are treated as a regular user of the Bolt Rider App. The experience of these business users is identical to that of regular users, except for the availability of an alternative payment option (Bolt Business) and an additional ride category (Business Ride). This may result in a scenario where, if a business customer deactivates and removes a business user's account, this individual will lose access to an alternative payment option (Bolt Business) and an additional ride category (Business Ride)._

_However, they will continue to be a customer of Bolt, which means Bolt will keep processing their personal data unless this individual decides to_ [+_request_+|https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/data-subject/] _data deletion or the data retention period specified in_ [+_Bolt`s privacy notices_+|https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/] _expires. In practical terms, this means that the personal data provided by business customers is  used to match newly added business users with the accounts of standard users. Individuals remain in control over their data._

_Additionally, as there had been a contractual relationship with the business customer, the data received from the business customer may be required for solving any dispute that may arise from the agreement with the business client. Deleting personal data on the request of business customers may deprive both Bolt and the individual from the opportunity to defend or substantiate their claims in the event that any claims should arise. Therefore, the data will be stored by Bolt as a data controller for the above stated purposes unless this individual decides to_ [+_request_+|https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/data-subject/] _data deletion or the data retention term provided by the law (limitation period for possible claims) expires, as outlined in the applicable_ [+_Bolt`s privacy notices_+|https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/]_._

_Please note that the notion of controllership in our arrangement is cemented by the_[ |https://edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/guidelines-072020-concepts-controller-and-processor-gdpr_en][+_EDPB Guidelines 07/2020_+|https://edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/guidelines-072020-concepts-controller-and-processor-gdpr_en] _on the concepts of controller and processor in the GDPR. Specifically, p. 27 para. 82 demonstrates this via “_*_Example: Taxi service”_*_. While Bolt operates as an online platform rather than providing taxi services directly, the example still effectively clarifies the logic underpinning the controller relationship._

_We appreciate your attention and trust that this explanation has clarified any concerns or questions you may have.”_

Thank you for your request!

To answer your question directly, the current guidelines are not really far from the truth on how agents should handle such cases. The article states that:

{quote}* If equipped to deal with the issue yourself, handle the non-safety part once the safety investigation is concluded.
* If not equipped to deal with such an issue, de-escalate the case to Tier 1 (keeping *both* the Severity level and the Safety issue tag/s) once you conclude the safety investigation.{quote}

So, it's as you mentioned, the agent should solve safety first, then deal with the non-safety issue. There is no necessity to escalate the case anywhere in a situation where the agent is equipped to deal with the non-safety part, so there’s no mention of it in the article. 

If the case contains a safety issue, no safety issue tags should be removed in either of the scenarios. The safety tags remain. If there’s a non-safety issue as well, then in both scenarios, the respective non-safety tags should be added to the case. 

Regarding who needs to add the tags - that is also clarified at the beginning of the article, specifically for cases that require escalation/de-escalation: 

{quote}* *Safety agents* are responsible for adding/removing only Safety issue tags when escalating/de-escalating a case. A non-safety agent will add non-safety issue tags.
* *Non-safety agents* are responsible for adding/removing only non-safety issue tags when escalating/de-escalating a case. A Safety agent will add the relevant Safety issue tags.{quote}

So, if the agent is equipped to solve the non-safety issue as well, the agent is also responsible for adding the relevant tags, as no de-escalation should take place. 

I agree that there is potential to adjust the wording for it to be more explicit, but right now, I don’t see that any changes would be needed to the process itself. Please correct me if I’m missing something or misunderstood. 

Additionally, together with the Process Excellence and Risk & Safety teams, we're currently working on revamping safety workflows, including the escalation guidelines. I will mark the need to make the guidelines more clear as something to consider when the new guidelines/workflows are drafted. 💭 

I will close the ticket, but if there’s anything else on this topic, feel free to use it for further communication. 

Have a nice day! 🙂

If you would create a new portfolio then later on you could also merge your portfolios to one. See [Carta guide for that|https://support.carta.com/s/article/merging-portfolios].

*Data Subject Access Request – Response* 

 

Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on 14 May 2024.

 

After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person. 

 

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software.Furthermore, we must point out that if after careful analysis we conclude that our rights or rights of others prevail,  we will not be able to provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.

 

We will share copies of the personal data we hold about *you* to which you are entitled. This includes:

* *Trip history data*

 

For information on how we process relevant personal data, we refer you to our Privacy Policy at [Terms and Conditions|https://bolt.eu/en/legal/] , which includes further information about:

* The categories of personal data we process;
* The purposes for which we process personal data;
* The recipients or categories of recipients to whom the personal data has been or will be disclosed;
* The criteria we use to determine how long to retain personal data;
* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* Your rights in relation to your personal data;
* The existence and envisaged consequences of any automated decision-making/profiling of personal data; and
* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.

 

*Your rights* 

 

In addition to your right to access any personal data we hold about you, you have the right to request us to rectify, erase your personal data, restrict the processing of your personal data or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 

 

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.

 

If you have any additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this email.

 

 

Yours sincerely,



Bolt

Hello Sam, 



Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on May 6th, 2024.



After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your request, we have determined that we do not process personal data in relation to your location between April 21, 2024 to April 29, 2024. 

We take your privacy seriously. As a part of this commitment, we would like to clarify our practices of collecting your location information. 

We start collecting your location data when you grant your permission for tracking it ‘All time', ‘While using the App’ or ‘Once’ via the application that refers to the settings on your devices. We ask for permission on sign in; however, such permission can be revoked or granted at any time via your device settings either when a prompt to authorise background use is displayed in the Bolt app or on your own. Your location is collected only in the foreground. It means that we start collecting your location data when you open the Bolt app and stop collecting it when you close the Bolt app. 

The permission to share your location data ‘All the time’ applies only to the geofencing feature which is used to notify you if we are operating in the specific area. We do not, however, store any of your location data in relation to this. iOS and Android devices enable apps to automatically trigger notifications when the user enters a specific geographical area. This does not require for the Bolt app to run in the background or mobile data to be used. Apple and Android store this information at their end and automatically trigger those notifications when a user enters a defined area, without sharing the user’s location with Bolt. 

For information on how we process relevant personal data, we refer you to our Privacy Policy at [https://bolt.eu/en-gb/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides|https://bolt.eu/en-gb/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides|smart-link] .

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.

 

If you have any additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this email.



Yours sincerely,

Bolt

Hi [~accountid:61dd8fc3f63ac80070cdf28a],

Since the rental of electric scooters takes place in a public place, *companies must have a permit from the Police Authority*, according to the Public Order Act (Sw. _ordningslagen_), *to use public space to display electric scooters*.

Our current permit in Stockholm *expires on June 30, 2024*. The terms attached to such permit states that the permit is only valid for the time set out in the agreement and that *should we not have a valid permit, we will be reported to the Police Authority* by the City of Stockholm. This means that if we do not get a new permit in time, we cannot keep the scooters in the public space, as this will violate the terms of the agreement with the City of Stockholm and could lead to them reporting us to the Police Authority.

The permit application is processed by the Police Authority and they are currently having longer processing times than normal. The Public Order Act does not include any information or guidance on how long the processing times by the Police Authority may be. However, as the Police Authority is an authority they are covered by the Administrative Procedure Act (Sw. _förvaltningslagen_). *The Administrative Procedure Act states that a matter shall be handled as simply, rapidly and cost-effectively as possible* without neglecting legal security.

There is, however, no guidance on how long the Police Authority may take to process a matter, as this must be assessed in each individual matter. *There is further no limit on when the Police Authority must complete the assessment of the application*.

Given that the Police Authority is not obliged to process the application before the current permit expires *we have no ground for a law suit against the Police Authority*. Pursuing litigation will be very costly and not successful. Further, such law suit will likely be *very damaging from a PR perspective*.

Also, there is no possibility to pursue litigation against the City of Stockholm as they are not involved in the permit application process.

*Our recommendation* is therefore that Public Policy ([~accountid:712020:36cbea54-0723-40fc-a8d1-2d4945acece1]) continue its dialogue with the authorities and closely monitor how the situation precedes during June. We further recommend that any recommendations from the City of Stockholm in this regard, should be followed. Should the City of Stockholm inform that we will most likely receive the new permit a few days after the current one has expired, they could inform that such vehicles could stay anyway (regardless of not having the permit). However, this is not for Legal to advise on. 

*To summarise*, we recommend not taking any legal actions and await and see if we will get at new permit in time. Public Policy should continue its dialogue with the authorities.

Hey Ioana-Andreea ,

In order to create base fee calculators, we would need the following information:

* *Commission rate*: Commission percentage that will apply per ride to the driver/fleet.
* *Currency*: Usually country default if not stated otherwise
* *Invoicing strategy*: Driver or Company. This will define to whom payouts will go, and invoices will be issued.
* *Booking fee:* Is there an active booking fee in the city? If so, do you want it to be deducted from the driver (and reflected on the commission invoice), or be a 100% driver income?
* *Cash-blocking thresholds*: Defines the cash ride limits for blocking/unblocking cash rides for a driver. This can be copied from other cities, but please discuss with [{color:#b3f5ff}Billing Analytics{color}|https://taxify.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/3/group/1240/create/806] if your market is cash-heavy.
** Max negative balance before messaging: The threshold where we will notify the driver that they are getting closer to being cash-blocked
** Max negative balance before removing cash payments: The debt threshold we allow cash rides up to. After the driver exceeds this threshold, cash orders will be disabled.
** Minimal balance to unblock cash rides: The balance threshold where we will once again unblock the driver’s cash rides.
* *List of company_ids you want this fee calculator to be attached to*.

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
*What is a Base Fee Calculator*

It is a default fee calculator template created by Billing team in order for local operations teams to easily attach the relevant fee calculator to new companies. [Please read this guide to see how|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/COMM/pages/1603928517/Base+fee+calculators].
{panel}

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
Make sure to make such requests at least 3 days in advance to have buffer for gathering this information
{panel}

Hi [~accountid:712020:ab95f96b-73f1-4bb8-a5fd-5178ef3f1339]

Please see some points below:

* At face value it seems unnecessary for Bolt to force drivers to have a higher insurance coverage than what is required by law, which thinking about it is something that also could be used to suggest a degree of subordination as pointed out by [~accountid:612f31d89976c300693ebaf7] . 
* We need to check the regulations in PT and the extend of the joint liability in the TVDE law to understand whether the decrease of the insurance coverage would entail risks for Bolt (maybe not). Relevant regulations in TVDE law:
** article 12(6) TVDe law: _6 - Without prejudice to the other insurances required by law, vehicles carrying out TVDE must have civil liability and personal accident insurance, which includes the passengers carried and their respective losses, in an amount not less than the minimum legally required for the activity of car hire._
** article 20(1) - _The electronic platform operator is jointly and severally liable to users for the punctual fulfilment of the obligations resulting from the contract._
* According to [~accountid:62a3287576c0360069f59b72] For context, all vehicles themselves will have to have Motor Third Party Liability (MTPL) as per the EU’s Motoring directive. However, each country sets its own minimum limits. For example:-
** The UK is Unlimited for Bodily injuries and £20m for property
** Germany is €7.5 million per person for bodily injuries and €1.12 million for property.  But most insurers provide €15m as standard.
* Now in Portugal the minimum requirement is currently €6.07m for Bodily injuries and €1.22 for Property. However, most Portuguese insurers provide higher limits of ~€10m for Bodily and €3m for Property.This MTPL coverage will pay for any damages caused by the motor vehicle. So the Civil liability being asked for is for incidents outside of the vehicle or not involving the vehicle; but are connected to the activity of a Ride Hailing service. E.g. Imagine a driver took you expensive Louis Vuitton case out the boot and ripped it on the pavement, this Civil liability could pay for these damages.Therefore, asking to have €50m seems very excessive to me for two reasons:
*# It is x5+ the limits provided under a vehicle insurance policy and a vehicle to me can cause a lot more damage.
*# It is excessive when compared to other places like the UK, France an Belgium ect. who only mandate €5m.

 [~accountid:62a3287576c0360069f59b72] can discuss this matter in detail with you since he might engage with insurance companies to attempt lower insurance costs.

So we can move forward with getting a green light to implement a process with CS Safety, we need Privacy to investigate the scope more in depth to understand under which circumstances we wish to take action, what action precisely and how we should communicate with our users in these instances.



*Question: Under which circumstances would we like to initiate a user-facing safety investigation?*

Answer: If the Police have requested data from Bolt and they’ve specified an incident has taken place on the Bolt platform/during a journey. This could include any safety event categorised by the Risk Team in Legal, but will most likely include events of a High/ Significant risk type (if the Police are involved). Sharing Rides safety events as an example [here|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/2404679884/Ride-Hailing+Safety+Standard+Operating+Procedures]. 



*Question: What action would we like to take as part of a user-facing investigation? How would we communicate with our users in these instances?*

Answer: CS Safety investigations usually involve blocking the alleged suspect (whether it’s a rider, driver, courier, eater etc) for the duration of the investigation and contacting both users involved, to find out what happened and to address the allegations with the reported user. 

The specific questions agents would ask can depend on the incident being reported. However, to give you a little idea as to what the comms might include, I will provide an example of the questions asked when handling a sexual assault incident:



{quote}*Queries for the reporting user:*

* Ask the reporting user to describe how the incident escalated;
* When it is unclear if the reporting party makes the report on their behalf or on behalf of a third party, consider checking with them if the victim was a third person;
* Ask the reporting user if the event has been reported to the police:
** If it has been reported to the police, *ask for the police reference number.* Log the reference number in the Tool under the Description of Events section.
** If the police report has not been made, *advise them to do so and forward us the reference number.*
* In addition, ask for the following information to identify the order if not already provided:
** Screenshot of the trip in their Bolt app;
** The date and time of the trip;
** The phone number of the reporting user.



*Queries for the reported user:*

* Inform the reported user about the suspension of their account.
** _"Your account has been blocked due to some irregular activities. We will contact you again shortly with more information"_
* For the first 24h from when the trip ended do not share any more information with the driver (do not provide them with the date).
* After 24h have passed, you can address the allegation, including the date, but it is essential to paraphrase it in a professional manner, refraining from using slang or sharing excessive details. While it's important to address the allegation, confidentiality must be maintained and specific information from the report cannot be shared, as that might endanger the police investigation and/or public safety.
** Example: _“According to the report we have received, you were involved in an alleged assault of sexual nature”_{quote}



Contact attempts with both users would begin with a phone call in Safety. If there’s no reply, the CS Safety agent will proceed with a written message to collect the same information. 

Once we have statements from both users, we can move forward with documenting and concluding the investigation from our side. The event is logged in the Cognito Tool including information about our findings, the reported user’s history and whether we are able to confirm this incident taking place. The Cognito Tool will then suggest an outcome for the reported user. This can be Education, Warning, Temp Block (1, 3, 7 or 28-days) or their Bolt account being suspended permanently. CS Safety will follow the guidelines and will communicate the outcome to the reported user in written form.

[~accountid:60f2a71843c956007065f2ad], please see our argument below:

Bolt aims to comply with local regulations requiring age verification for the rental of individual electric vehicles while maintaining a strong commitment to privacy and data protection. The requirement to scan or photograph identity documents (IDs) introduces significant privacy concerns and may not be the least intrusive method for achieving the regulatory objective. We argue that existing measures, including the use of bank account information, adequately ensure that users meet the age requirement, thus fulfilling the principle of data minimisation under the the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

*Legal framework*. GDPR mandates that personal data collection must be limited to what is directly relevant and necessary to achieve a specific purpose (Article 5(1)(c)). Collecting IDs for age verification is excessively intrusive and not strictly necessary when less invasive methods are available. The proportionality principle under GDPR requires that data processing measures are balanced against the need to protect individuals' privacy rights. ID documents contain sensitive personal information that goes beyond the scope of age verification, thus we assert that the processing of personal identifiers through ID verification is disproportionate when compared to other available methods.

*Existing Age Verification Mechanism*. Bolt already requires users to enter bank account details as part of the registration process. Bank accounts are generally restricted to individuals who are 18 years or older. Financial institutions have robust age verification processes in place, ensuring that the bank account holder is of legal age or has the necessary consent. Additionally, users must agree to Bolt’s Terms and Conditions, which stipulate compliance with local and national regulations, including age requirements. This agreement acts as a contractual obligation for users to confirm their age.

Bolt respectfully submits that the current practice of verifying age through bank account information is both effective and compliant with the principle of data minimisation under GDPR. The introduction of ID verification controls is unnecessarily intrusive and presents significant privacy risks. By leveraging existing financial institution verifications, Bolt ensures regulatory compliance while protecting user privacy, thus aligning with both local regulations and GDPR principles.

We urge the City Hall to consider the sufficiency of Bolt’s current age verification method and recognise the importance of data minimisation in protecting user privacy.

Hi [~accountid:712020:0b1ccfcb-3809-460a-88ab-c96985ba329a] - thanks for this. I’ve taken a look at the latest version of Seismic’s DPA (attached in the thread below) and my main thoughts are as follows:

* I have included in the table below some general suggestions regarding provisions on: (1) *indemnities*; (2) *engaging sub-processors*; (3) notifying Bolt of *data subject requests*; and (4) notifying Bolt of *personal data breaches*. I appreciate that these do not concern the AI feature, but seeing as Lighthouse are preparing a full RFR, I thought I should flag them for completeness.
* Re the AI feature, my gut reaction is that *the relevant processing activities are not adequately covered by the DPA*. I can understand Seismic’s argument that _technically_ they are covered insofar as the language is quite broad / all-encompassing (and so this is not a huge risk), but to protect Bolt’s position I have recommended some additions that could be made to Exhibit A.

As previously discussed, if we are proposing edits to this DPA, then we should fold these into the discussion re [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-35259|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-35259|smart-link]. Let’s discuss both at the same time on Monday.



||*Issue*||*Suggestion(s)*||
|*Indemnity*
The DPA does not appear to place any specific obligation on Seismic (as processor) to indemnify Bolt (as controller) for any failure by Seismic (or its sub-processors / employees) to comply with its obligations. I also cannot see any such indemnity in the SaaS agreement.|Unless there is a business reason why we have not previously sought one, I assume we should push for such an indemnity to be included in the DPA?|
|*Engaging Sub-processors*
*Clause 4.6* of the DPA states that when entering into agreements with sub-processors, Seismic must impose “comparable” obligations on the sub-processors. This is not the standard required by Article 28(4) GDPR, which states that the obligations must be “the same”.|To meet the higher threshold under Article 28(4), and to align with the advice in our [contracting playbook|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/4499439674/Data+Protection+Contracting+Playbook], I recommend we change “comparable” to “the same, in substance”.|
|*Notification deadlines*
*Clause 7.1* of the DPA states that Seismic should notify Bolt if it receives a data subject rights request (“DSRR”). However, it does not place a specific time limit on Seismic to do so. 

Similarly, *Clause 8.6* states that Seismic should notify Bolt of personal data breaches “without undue delay”.|To align with the advice in our [contracting playbook|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/4499439674/Data+Protection+Contracting+Playbook], I recommend we impose a time limit of between 24 hours and 3 business days for Seismic to notify Bolt of any relevant DSRRs. 

Again, to align with the advice in our [contracting playbook|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/4499439674/Data+Protection+Contracting+Playbook], I recommend we impose a time limit of between 24 and 48 hours.|
|*AI Feature*
The *purposes* of processing listed in *Exhibit A* do not explicitly include the generation of content by the AI feature (nor training the AI feature, which may also be going on here).




The *categories of personal data* in *Exhibit A* (in particular, the table) do not cover / envision a scenario in which Bolt provides a different type of personal data to the AI feature for the purpose of generating content. Also, Exhibit A explicitly says that no special category data will be processed - technically, someone from Bolt could accidentally provide such information to the AI feature when asking it to generate content.





It is possible that someone from Bolt could provide the AI feature with the personal data of someone who is not included in the *categories of data subjects* listed in *Exhibit A*.|This is *low risk*, as the broad purpose of processing in the DPA is “provision of the Services”, which could be construed as including the AI feature. However, this might be a stretch, as given that the AI feature is new, it is not explicitly mentioned in the SaaS agreement (which defines “Services”). As such, it might be worth including a reference to the purpose of generating content on the platform - let me know what you think.

Again, this is *low risk*, as Exhibit A says Seismic may process “any Personal Data provided by [Bolt]”. Also, it is not guaranteed that any categories of personal data beyond those listed in the table would be provided by Bolt to the AI feature. Nevertheless, to mitigate the risk of someone from Bolt providing the AI feature with information beyond what is listed in the table, it could be worth including an extra row to the effect of “Any other Personal Data provided by Customer to Company in order to provide the Services” - what do you think? On the special category data point, I think the most sensible solution here would be to make sure that no-one from the Bolt side provides the AI feature with such information in the first place.

As above, this is *low risk*, and could either be dealt with by: (a) including a row in this table to cater for “Any other individuals whose Personal Data are provided by Customer to Company in order to provide the Services”; and/or (b) ensuring on the Bolt side that we do not provide too much personal data to the AI feature - keen to hear your thoughts.|

*In summary*, I would be grateful  if we could discuss the exact nature of the relationship between the partner market entities (“PMEs”) and suppliers like Seismic (I have asked a follow-up question to Viktoriia already on this basis), but if I have understood it correctly then my immediate thoughts are as follows:

# Assuming that the PMEs would be signing up to the DPA, *more edits are needed* than just changing the definition of ‘Customer’ to include ‘Customer’s Partners'. For example, we would also likely need to change defined terms like ‘Data Protection Legislation’ and ‘Supervisory Authority’, as well as add in new substantive provisions.
# We may need *local counsel input* from Mexico / Georgia / Saudi Arabia to get an idea of the relevant restrictions on international data transfers, as *further exhibits to the DPA may be needed* (dealing with transfer mechanisms).
# From a practicality perspective, if the PMEs were all party to the DPA, it is *not entirely clear who the responsible Bolt / PME entities would be* in situations involving data subject rights requests / responding to personal data breaches. Do we have a standard approach that we would ordinarily take in these kinds of situations?

*(1)* +*Edits to the DPA*+

If the PMEs will also be party to the DPA, then from an initial review it appears that the following edits to the DPA would be needed:

* If the definition of “Customer” in the SaaS agreement is being amended to include “Customer’s Partners”, then I would be minded to *remove the definition of “Customer” from the DPA altogether* (and instead just include the _term_ “Customer”). This is because the DPA says “_any terms not defined in this DPA shall have the meaning set forth in the Agreement_” - so it would be an easier uplift just to remove the definition from the DPA (and rely on the SaaS definition) rather than include a full suite of new defined terms in the DPA. Alternatively, we could just include the new definitions / defined terms, but this is extra work.
* Given that the partner markets (which we are aware of) include Austria, Hungary, Georgia, Saudi Arabia and Mexico, I would *update the definition of “Data Protection Legislation”* as follows, to ensure that there markets are included:
** (1) Change “_any applicable laws and regulations in any relevant jurisdiction relating to the use or processing of Personal Data including_” to “_any applicable laws and regulations in any relevant jurisdiction relating to the use or processing of Personal Data including,_ +_but not limited to_+”; and
** (2) Include two extra roman numerals before “_in each case, as updated, amended or replaced from time to time_” saying: “_(_+_vii) the EU GDPR as it forms part of the national law of each EU Member State; and (viii) any equivalent laws in any other part of the world, each to the extent applicable to the parties_+”.
* We should consider *defining “Supervisory Authority”more definitively*. Currently, this term is defined according to the GDPR, whose definition refers only to authorities established in Member States. As such, this technically would not cover authorities established in Mexico, Saudi Arabia and Georgia. We might want to change it to something like “a supra-national, national or sub-national authority, commission, department, agency, regulator or regulatory body with jurisdiction over data protection matters in any jurisdiction whose laws are applicable to the Customer”.
* We would likely need to *make edits to the international data transfer provisions* (i.e., clause 6) to cover data transfers coming out of Mexico / Georgia / Saudi Arabia.

*(2)* +*Exhibits / Transfer Mechanisms*+

If the PMEs will also be party to the DPA, then data transfers out of Mexico, Georgia and Saudi Arabia are not currently covered in the DPA. *Subject to local counsel advice* (let me know if we have already obtained this as part of a separate project), my gut reaction would be that we need to either: (a) *implement additional transfer mechanisms* / exhibits in this DPA; or (b) get the entities from the relevant partner markets to enter into separate DPAs. Could we have a chat about this , so I can get some insight into how we would usually approach this sort of issue?

*(3)* +*Responsible entities*+

Certain provisions regarding dealing with data subject requests and personal data breaches require Seismic to notify the “Customer”, who then has responsibility to resolve the matter. If the PMEs become party to the DPA, it is not entirely clear to me how these responsibilities would be allocated. Let’s discuss on our sync on this.

Hey [~accountid:712020:81ed6d45-d7b2-45d4-89cd-030f00488538],

Picking this up from Sam. Brief summary is as follows:

* The section of the GDPR that Mare is referring to is *Article 9*.
* *Could you please provide some more information on what exactly the “disclosures” envisioned in rows 27-34 of the table will look like* (in particular, whether Bolt will only be disclosing _aggregated statistics_ that cannot be used to identify specific individuals)? This will determine whether we actually need to be concerned by Article 9 of the GDPR.

I have set out a bit more detail below. Hopefully this is a helpful overview - please let me know if you need any further info / analysis and I would be happy to help.



+*Article 9 GDPR*+

Article 9 says that Bolt cannot use or collect any ‘sensitive’ personal data unless an exception applies. By sensitive personal data, we mean *racial or ethnic origin* (which is relevant to row 29 of the table), political opinions, *religious / philosophical beliefs* (which could be relevant to row 30, although it is not entirely clear), trade union membership, genetic / biometric data, *health data* (which would include disabilities - this is therefore relevant to row 30 of the table), and data concerning a person’s *sex life or sexual orientation* (which is relevant to row 30 of the table)

Other categories of information listed in the D&I rows of the table (e.g., gender and age in rows 27-28 and 31-34) are +not+ considered sensitive in this context, and so are not caught by this restriction.

Bolt does collect and use some of these categories of personal data from its workforce. For example, Bolt’s employee privacy notice ([https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/BILP/pages/3483271278/Bolt+Employee+Privacy+Notice|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/BILP/pages/3483271278/Bolt+Employee+Privacy+Notice|smart-link]) mentions how Bolt can collect disability information.

Article 9 then goes on to list the specific circumstances (i.e., ‘exceptions’) in which Bolt _can_ collect and use such information (e.g., Bolt can do so where it has obtained the person’s explicit consent, where Bolt is discharging obligations under employment / social protection law etc.). I can provide some more detailed info on this if helpful.



+*Note - Aggregated Statistics*+

If I understand your summary correctly, it looks like Bolt might end up disclosing statistics that are relevant to certain sensitive categories of information (e.g., "the proportion of its total direct operations workforce for each employee category by race or ethnicity"). If these statistics are aggregated and cannot be used to identify specific people, then they will not contain any personal data, and the GDPR (including the restrictions in Article 9 set out above) will not apply. For example:

* “X% of Bolt employees are Christian” - Does not reveal which specific individuals at Bolt are Christian. Does not contain personal data. GDPR restrictions do not apply.
* “John Doe (Operations Manager at Bolt) is Christian. Jane Doe (Product Specialist at Bolt) is Muslim” - Information relates to specific individuals, and so is personal data. GDPR restrictions apply (including Article 9).

In other words, if Bolt meeting the social commitments only involves disclosing aggregated statistics, then this would not raise any issues from a privacy perspective. *Could you therefore provide any more information on what the disclosures will look like?*

Hey!

# Demand-based pricing is legal and used in car- and ride-sharing services. The prices are shown before the consumer activates the service (scooter session) and they are aware of the current price. Price components are shown in the Bolt app. If a person does not agree to the displayed prices, there are different alternatives for the service - including other scooters or ride-hailing services.
# The speed reductions are made based on the input from the municipality as this is something that Bolt cannot decide independently - if the municipality decides to reduce the maximum speed for operations, we have to comply with this as this is the requirement for operating the service in the municipality. In addition, we have some areas where the scooters cannot operate at all or operate at even more reduced speeds. This goes for all the municipalities in Latvia (for example, see the speed-restricted areas in Jelgava or Daugavpils). If the municipality sets additional restrictions (for example: speed limits during public holidays, near schools, during nighttime time etc), we implement the restrictions as the municipality sets them. As a general remark - it’s common practice to limit the speed in parks (in Europe) and different cities set different speed limits, but as a general rule, they are between 5-15 km/h.
# GPS will always have some margin of error for determining the exact location of the receiver and this can be affected by different factors, from cloud cover to signal reflection. If the user isn’t able to finish the ride, we ask them to contact customer support so we can do this manually. The restrictions on the scooter’s location are quite narrow as the same hardware is used in countries where the scooter’s location has to be within 1-2 cm of the parking area. The future versions of the hardware will be equipped with more precise GPS receivers, but they are not immune to disturbances. 

If he wishes to claim something, then he can submit the claim to our official email address. The scooter service is operated by Bolt Operations OÜ.

If he wishes to submit the complaint to the consumer protection agency, the contacts are listed here: [https://www.ptac.gov.lv/lv/iestades-kontakti|https://www.ptac.gov.lv/lv/iestades-kontakti|smart-link]

Hey [~accountid:6012ba328fb6ea014a8294ce] (cc. [~accountid:6149a0e9ba1b34006ab04897] [~accountid:610a3ee66051c5006aeeeea1]) - generally speaking, unless the adverts are extremely intrusive and annoying, it would be inappropriate to *_insist_* that drivers remove these devices - that has the effect of restricting the drivers' own economic activities. We should be careful to avoid insisting on any behaviours that apply when drivers are not providing services via the platform. 

With that said, there are a few approaches that could be used to persuade (or ‘soft force’) drivers to remove the devices. However they are either (i) circumstantial, (ii) risk upsetting our relationship with the drivers/fleets, (iii) will require fully off-boarding the drivers (affecting supply) and/or (iv) will require the local team to play around with category requirements.

As that’s the case it is not obvious to me that any of these approaches are worth the effort - but that’s a decision for the commercial teams to make based on how damaging to our brand these screens are. Regardless, here are the options:

*(1)* If the drivers have a branding / advertising agreement with Bolt, then Bolt say these screens clash with our values and drivers can choose between our branding / advertising arrangement (“we’ll need to end our arrangement with you unless…”. There are some templates to that effect [{color:#ff5630}here{color}|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1b4mKiScPZgmGwlHKLT9rTcfDTVUGPkLjQE-S5M5wCSo/edit#heading=h.p2klrmn81hl1] which will need adapting. Obviously this is a bit awkward if Bolt has previously promoted these screens, but overall this is probably the ‘least sensitive’ approach. 

*(2)* If the screens are legitimately deeply annoying to passengers, these fleets/drivers could be warned that they will be suspended from the platform if they are not removed. This approach requires some sort of ‘data’ that passengers dislike these adverts, plus there being a ‘do not cause nuisance’ provision in our T+Cs (which may not be the case in ES).

*(3)* If the adverts were grossly offensive or considered inappropriate (advertising gambling / adult content etc.) Bolt could unilaterally take action on the basis that the driver is causing some sort of ‘harm’. This would require us pinning this to a clause in local terms. This feels like a stretch. 

*(4)* If Bolt does not have the benefit of a ‘do not cause nuisance / do not offend’ clause, Bolt could ‘request’ that the screens are removed (restating that it does not consider that these accord with the brand) and warn that it will have to terminate its relationship with the fleet/driver. The terminations would then be on the basis of termination for convenience - 30 days' notice (“we’ve decided that this does not work for us”).

*(5)*  Bolt could change its premium category criteria to reflect ‘a premium ride experience with no adverts’ - this will force the existing drivers out of the premium categories unless they lose their screens. Obviously a driver that remains in just the standard categories would be unaffected. 

Thanks 🙏

Hi [~accountid:6012ba328fb6ea014a8294ce] - it’s hard to see how that would work in practice. 

For these arrangements to have the desired effect, it would have to effectively require the driver/fleet to effectively ‘cease’ advertising. This may be seen as: (i) ‘buying exclusivity’ in respect of branding/advertising (i.e. you must have no advertising), and/or (ii) agreeing a blanket prohibition on advertising. 

In each case, this sort of micromanagement goes beyond Bolt’s role in acting _for_ the driver in the provision of the platform and is, generally speaking, inappropriate. Engaging in branding in the first place starts introducing risks in the market - which Bolt has accepted; adding ‘buying exclusivity’ into the mix makes the position less favourable still. If Bolt were to engage in this activity it would have to aim to be very discrete.

Also, exercising that strategy would be ‘energy expensive’ in terms of set-up, framing/drafting the settlement, payouts and monitoring. There is also a question of sustainability; if this practice of ‘paying off drivers’ became common knowledge it may actually incentivise the use of screens.

Finally, such an ‘offer’ couldn’t be considered an incentive in the typical sense (VAT would need considering).

+*Overall*+: Bolt should only consider ‘paying off’ these fleets/drivers if (i) the negative impact of the screens is considered very high, (ii) we think the ‘deal’ could be executed discretely, (iii) there is not a looming threat of reclass action in the market (which is a question for the local team), (iv) the need to take action outweighs the cost / support team resource (which is a question for the local business team).

All things considered, it does not seem like a worthwhile strategy to me but it’s something the central / local business teams could agree to pursue if they are willing to dedicate the resource to it and accept the impacts.

Adding on to that, I understand your approach would be to _“pay them each month for 'ad free' car”_.

It’s hard to see how this would scale: drivers that don’t have these screens may be quite frustrated to hear that some drivers have the benefit of this, so there is a risk of causing negative driver sentiment. If it applied to the _whole_ set of drivers in the market, then Bolt would effectively be paying all drivers to restrict their own economic activities, which doesn’t seem a good idea for most markets.

All things considered, my recommended approaches would be:

*(1 - most recommended)* Do nothing. If there is scope to get comfortable then this seems to the way forward. The screen situation is not ideal, but Bolt cannot act without increasing its risk profile and spending time/energy to resolve. I’m also factoring in that there is a soft benefit in allowing some branding/advertising to occur in some capacity (as set out in the headline branding strategy note aimed at management - [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1b4mKiScPZgmGwlHKLT9rTcfDTVUGPkLjQE-S5M5wCSo/edit#heading=h.p2klrmn81hl1]).

*(2)* Give drivers the choice of Bolt’s branding agreement or removing their screens (i.e. this seems a better approach to me than ‘paying a bonus to remove the screens’). The local legal team may have a different view to me on this (cc. [~accountid:6149a0e9ba1b34006ab04897] / [~accountid:610a3ee66051c5006aeeeea1]).

All of the strategies, including ‘do nothing’, have pros and cons. There is room to proceed with any of them if the ‘pros’ are compelling enough, so long as the corresponding negatives are carefully considered by the central/local business teams.

Hi all!

I have assessed the documentation provided by Google on the feature, and I can say that overall our considerations remain the same. Even though the data that is shared with Google is hashed, the activity itself still involves personal data processing, as we must first collect information of the drivers and compile a Customer Data file before it gets hashed and is sent to Google.

*Preliminary conclusions:*

Formally, to make this activity lawful, we would need:

* document the new purpose, the lawful basis (legitimate interest - recognised in Ghana as well), retention period - the basic details of this new data processing activity;
* inform the drivers re/ this and provide to them these details.

This is both under the GDPR and the Ghanian privacy laws. Unfortunately, our privacy notices are currently silent on any promotional/marketing activities that we may run - this is an oversight that is currently being mitigated, as we are preparing to roll out updated privacy notices for drivers in the coming months.

I would say that with the updated privacy notices, we would be covered, and the activity could be run without any risk.

However, if you choose to run the activity before this, the risks should be low, because:

* the activity is limited to Accra and will only concerns a limited number of driver profiles that will be used to compile the Customer Data file;
* the risks under the Ghanian laws are low as the activity of the regulator should be low there;
* the risks under the GDPR are also low as the activity is in Ghana, and though the GDPR has extraterritorial reach, the regulatory GDPR risks for activities outside of the EU are generally low.

Hey [~accountid:712020:822a759a-daf0-4161-afbf-8b79a2985fba] while similar I believe there is a slight difference to this 

(i) Delivery related arrangement here 

compared to 

(ii) the Business Coupons one.

*In both cases* there is a provider of benefits platform (e.g. _Edenred_, Juno, Coverflex) who typically has partnered with a FinReg licensed third party (e.g. Adyen, or the PrePay here) so that dedicated cards could be issued to the users (typically _employees_) of Edenred’s b2b clients (typically _employers_). 

Under a basic scenario such employer would contract with Edenred and set limits and/or policies on Edenred’s platform regarding what products and services _from which_ (_third party) merchants available on Edenred’s platform_ can be purchased with the card. And then the employees would go on and purchase the services from the merchants using the card.

Meaning, *under the arrangement at hand Bolt would merely be another merchant on Edenred’s platform* under this scheme. It seems we wouldn’t have any direct arrangement with the employers, but can treat the employees as our regular users [eaters], and the card as any other card a user would add to the eater app which we’d charge upon order. The request at hand seems to be about adding a further layer, i.e. a contract between us and Edenred so that we could continue to have access to their demand base, and so that they could get a commission for that.

*Now in these other cases which involve Bolt Business and namely its Coupons feature* I see the matter being slightly more complex. Namely on top of the above Bolt would have a regular Bolt Business contract with Edenred in order for the latter to have access to the ability to generate and distribute the Coupons to the employees in the first place. Meaning Bolt would be providing Edenred the (Business account) SaaS for which it charges Business Service Fee. _I guess if cards are used then fees for rides we’d charge directly from users as above. If no cards are in play then we’d charge it from Edenred as our Business customer (postpaid mode)._ TBD how to facilitate the commission requested by Edenred from Bolt but I’d prefer a rebate from the Business Service Fee to maintain the narrative that Bolt is providing services to Edenred (not vice versa). 

More importantly, with the latter setup comes also FinReg risk per advice from Commerce Compliance - should Edenred collect funds from the employers before Coupons are even used for Bolt services. That’s storing value, and we shouldn’t make our offerings available via a platform which does not have the relevant license. *The Content*

h4. DVLA invalid

The data we have in Admin does not match with the online automated check, most commonly due to a change of name or address, or if the NIN is incorrect in our system

The driver’s account will be blocked with the blocking message _Bolt requires you to submit a DVLA check code to verify the validity of your DVLA Driver Licence. Please submit your DVLA Electronic Counterpart Check Code._

* Ask the driver to submit their DVLA check code via the form in the message
* Advise them that their account will be unblocked once the code is verified
** If the driver reports that they submitted their DVLA check code, but their account was not unblocked, or the driver sent the code via a ticket, escalate the case via the Service Desk to the [Reactivation team via Service Desk|https://taxify.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/35]
* Inform the driver that it will take up to 48 hours for us to get back with a reply or review their documents

h4. DVLA missing

* Ask the driver to submit their driving licence via the Driver Portal
* Advise them that their account will be unblocked once the document is verified
** If the driver reports they have submitted their driving licence, escalate the case to the local OPS team
* Inform the driver it will take up to 48 hours for us to get back with a reply or review their documents

h4. External checks

*Failed*

Our system runs our entire driver base against Transport for London’s online database daily. The driver’s profile will be blocked automatically if there are no results returned from the online database. There are two types of blocking reasons:

* External check failed {"type":"phv" <...>}: There is no valid Private Hire Vehicle Licence for the vehicle listed in brackets [NUMBER PLATE], or the PHV details do not match with the TfL database. The block will be automatically removed when a valid result is returned.
* External check failed {"type":"phl" <...>}: There is no valid Private Hire Driver Licence, or the PHL details do not match with the TfL database. The block will be automatically removed when a valid result is returned.
** Inform the driver about the reason why their account is blocked
** Advise them that their account will be unblocked when the needed document is proven by Transport for London

h4. Pending review blocks

After the activation, drivers will still be blocked for some time to run external checks before allowing them to start driving. The account will be unblocked when a PHV (Private Hire Vehicle Licence) and PHL (Private Hire Driver Licence) are checked with the Transport for London database.
	+ * Advise the driver that their account will be unblocked when the document verification is finished
	+ * If the scheduled block was placed incorrectly, escalate the case to  the [Technical Support team’s Service Desk|https://taxify.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/2]

h4. Car applications in the UK

<details>
<summary>New car application</summary>
<be>

When a driver submits a request to change their vehicle through the Driver Portal, they will temporarily be blocked until the new vehicle is approved. This block is meant to prevent drivers from operating when we know they have a different vehicle.

* Advise the driver that:
** The vehicle application is being processed
** When the new vehicle application is reviewed and activated, their account will be unblocked. 
** If we have to decline their vehicle application they will receive a notification to their registered email address.
* Check if the driver submitted documents by mistake and if the block has been active for over 48 hours	
** Escalate the case:
*** For *London* via the [Reactivation team's Service Desk|https://taxify.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/35]
*** For *Expansion* via the [Expansion Service Desk|https://taxify.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/31/create/528?src=1826823624]

</details>

<details>
<summary>Possible new car application</summary>
<be>

The driver’s profile will be blocked when they submit all vehicle documents within 15 minutes through Fleet Documents. The block is in place based on the assumption that the driver likely is submitting documents for a new vehicle, albeit through the wrong channel (Fleet Documents instead of Car Applications).

* Inform the driver about the reason why their account is blocked
* Advise them to submit a new vehicle application via the Driver Portal
* If the *driver submitted documents by mistake* and the block has been active for *over 48 hours*, escalate the case: 
** For *London* via the [Reactivation team's Service Desk|https://taxify.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/35]
** For *Expansion* via the [Expansion Service Desk|https://taxify.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/31/create/528?src=1826823624]
* Inform the driver that their documents will be reviewed as soon as possible.
</details>
